name: AISLE platform
operator: AISLE (the vendor); each customer is the operator of its own use
basis: AISLE's own public product, blog and about pages, and third-party vulnerability records (OpenSSL, curl, Samba) that credit its work
what: AISLE's platform of AI agents that finds vulnerabilities in source code, triages them, writes and tests patches, and delivers them as pull requests for people to merge.
note: A scan of a product as its vendor documents it, not of any one deployment. Made by the report studio: a researcher-assessor, a challenger, then the scorer.
grant_note: Not measured. No deployment shape for this product is published in the capability grammar.

findings.finding: The span is not in the source. The span reads 'AISLE finds, fixes, and verifies vulnerabilities autonomously'. The home page reads 'AISLE finds, fixes, and verifies vulnerabilities in your source code, at machine speed and scale.' The word 'autonomously' appears elsewhere on the page in a different sentence ('the sovereign AI platform that finds and fixes vulnerabilities, autonomously'). The span as written joins two sentences. The note ('finding, fixing and verifying vulnerabilities in source code') is supported by the real sentence, so the grade and mode are right; replace the span with the exact words 'finds, fixes, and verifies vulnerabilities in your source code'. I20 is not used for any card level, so the card does not change.

The note says the open-source page shows an 'aisle-security' bot account in a mock-up. That page is not among the scan's sources, and the string aisle-security does not appear in any of the ten fetched AISLE pages. Only the OpenSSL story is supported: it says 'Maintainers can trigger an AISLE review simply by tagging' the handle aisle-analyzer in inline comments. Either add the open-source page as a source with the quote, or drop that half of the note. Grade documented and mode deployed are acceptable as the story describes OpenSSL's real use, and the note already says the accounts were not checked on GitHub. I26 feeds no level on this card.

Arguing against A4. Rule: A4 needs level 3 (I08 plus one of I17, I18, I19), I10 or I12 or I13, and I18 or I19. Only I18 is credited from that set, so I18 carries both A3 and A4; remove it and Autonomy falls well below 3. The span 'All you do is review and merge.' is on the remediation page and is a marketing sentence. The artefacts behind it are firmer: the FAQ on that page says 'Can AISLE merge a fix without us? No.' with 'a human must review and merge', and the page says 'Nothing reaches your main branch until someone on your team merges it'. So 'person approves the critical decision only' holds for the merge step. The real weakness is the default. The triage page says 'AISLE can speed up your remediation flow by fixing every vulnerability, but it doesn't have to', and that the customer chooses per severity and repository 'where to stop at triage and where to speed through to a PR'. No page states which setting is the default for a new customer, so mode available is the cautious and correct choice; default would be overstated. The card shows A4 with avail 'available', which is honest. I10 rests on one statement: 'plugs into the scanners, repos, and CI you already run'. That is a statement of integration, not an artefact, and it names GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, so it is acceptable. Overall A4 rests on documented statements from the vendor with no observed operation, and its top step depends on the opt-in mode. Keep as is, but any display of A4 should keep the available flag visible.

The user asked about S1 as the base of A4: since Spectrum 0.2, S1 no longer feeds any Autonomy level (the indicator scope says so), it only earns the In production badge. A4 rests on I10 and I18, not S1. On S1 itself: the Productboard story names the customer and says it rolled out AISLE 'across all 56 repositories'. The span 'Jira ticket creation, Slack notifications, and AI-powered pull requests' is in the page and under fifteen words. But 56 repositories is a rollout scope, not sessions, tasks or pull requests, and the page gives no count of pull requests opened or merged. The only usage-style figures on the page are alert counts (30,000 alerts to 6). The page says the company 'integrated' AI-powered pull requests into its workflow, which names a customer for the acting capability but does not state that Productboard's pull requests were produced in practice. The scope allows a named customer, so the answer passes by the letter; the note should say plainly that no pull request or task count is published and that the named-customer limb is what is used. Grade documented, mode default: acceptable.

S4 is not answered. The scan lists under not_credited a read-only MCP server announced on an AISLE blog post, with the reason that it is an agent-to-tool interface over AISLE's data and not a protocol between agents. The S4 scope says a published MCP server counts, and only an interface the product merely consumes does not count. A server AISLE publishes for a customer's coding agent to call appears to match the scope. I could not read the blog URL (it returned nothing usable through curl, probably script-rendered), and it is not one of the scan's fetched sources, so I cannot confirm the page says it is published and callable. Needed: either add the blog post as a source with an exact span and credit S4 as documented (mode available, configuration mcp), or state why the scope is not met. As written the rejection reason does not match the scope text. This affects Reach, not Autonomy.

The enterprise FAQ says 'every finding and fix is logged from detection to verified fix to human-approved pull request, with timestamps and named approvers', and the remediation page lists 'Every AISLE action is traceable'. I41 needs operation and its scope wants a log of what the agent does; the answer is graded documented, so it does not count toward any level, which is correct. The note already says documented only, not observed. The log described covers findings and fixes, which is close to agent actions but not stated as tool calls or commits.

Opened the sources and checked each span in the page text and each note against it. I04: the FAQ says AISLE builds the repository in an isolated container, applies the patch and runs the tests. I08: writes a patch, runs the tests and opens a pull request. I10 and I11: integration with scanners, repos and CI, and connection to hosted version control, stated on the platform and discovery pages. I21: 'You decide how far AISLE goes on its own, per severity and per repository' is on the remediation page. I22: guidance instead of a patch for some findings, and a failing fix going back to the team, stated in the FAQ. I38: 'Nothing merges without human approval' and the no-merge FAQ answer. I57: contesting a triage decision is on the triage page. I58: privacy policy lists customer data. I67: enterprise page gives hours-saved figures; the note correctly says no method is published. I68: the deployment page states continuous updates for Managed SaaS and monthly for private cloud and on-prem; the note correctly says this is a cadence, not a process, and the 3-word span is within limits. All are documented, statement-type indicators, so no operation grade is needed; modes default are right as these are page statements of shipped behaviour. Credit to the indicators matches their text.

Card computed with node: A4 R2 C1 O2. A4 uses I10 and I18 (I18 flagged available). R2 uses I10 and I11, next unlocks I13 and S2. C1 uses I38 only, next I23. O2 uses I22 and I58, next I50. Levels 3 and 4 appear only in Autonomy. Every item behind them is a vendor statement graded documented; no operation was observed. The grant is stated as not measured, which is correct for a product kind. The scan is still a draft with no review rounds; the I20 span fix and the I26 source fix are needed before it moves on.

Credit is right in substance (round one finding answered in part). The span 'Developers can connect AISLE to AI agents that support the Model Context Protocol' is 13 words and exact in the October rollout post (fetched 10 November 2026); grade documented, mode available, cfg mcp, indicator S4 fit the scope. But the note states that the announcement post 'returned 404 on 10 November 2026' and was 'captured earlier'. When fetched by this reviewer the URL aisle.com/blog/announcing-the-aisle-mcp-server answered 200 with the full post titled 'Announcing the AISLE MCP Server'; it says the server is read-only, lists five tools (issue-list, issue-detail, issue-count, fix-list, repo-list) and gives sign-in by OAuth or a personal access token. The 404 claim is false as the page stands, and the page is no longer among the scan's captures, so 'five tools' cannot be checked from the scan. Needed: drop the 404 sentence, and either re-capture the announcement post and cite it (it is the stronger source for a published, callable interface) or keep only what the rollout post says. S4 does not change any level: Reach level three needs I25 as well, and removing S4 leaves the card A4 R2 C1 O2.

Two defects in the not_credited list after round one. (1) The entry 'OpenSSL, curl and Samba advisories credit vulnerabilities to researchers of Aisle Research' now appears twice, identical: the studio's edit duplicated it instead of only removing the MCP entry. Remove one. (2) The entry names curl and Samba, but its only source, the OpenSSL vulnerabilities page, contains 'Aisle Research' 40 times and the words curl and Samba zero times; no source of the scan supports curl or Samba. Either add a source for each or say only OpenSSL. The I26 mock-up entry is supported: aisle-security appears on aisle.com/open-source as a styled graphic, as the entry says, and I26 now rests on the OpenSSL story alone.

Card A4 R2 C1 O2 (S4 added changes nothing). Levels three and four are only in Autonomy, and I removed each fact in turn with node. Without I18 the Autonomy dimension is A- (no level at all, below the one-level floor), because I15, I16 and I07 are not credited and A2 has nothing else; without I08 it is also A-; without I10 the card is A3; without S4 it stays A4. So the whole Autonomy rating rests on I08 and the single fact I18. I18 is a vendor statement graded documented, and its span 'All you do is review and merge.' is a marketing line; the firmer artefacts are the FAQ 'Can AISLE merge a fix without us? No.' and 'Nothing reaches your main branch until someone on your team merges it', which show the human merge step, and the triage page 'it doesn't have to' shows that the customer chooses how far it goes. The default is not stated anywhere, so mode available is the honest choice and A4 must always be displayed with that flag; shown without it the card would claim a default behaviour no page states. A4 (I10 added) rests on one integration sentence, 'plugs into the scanners, repos, and CI you already run', naming GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket: a dated page statement, but not an operation. Nothing is observed or measured; the grade ceiling is documented for the whole card. Recommend the display say A4 is read from vendor statements and opt-in.

Verified against freshly fetched sources. I20: new span 'finds, fixes, and verifies vulnerabilities in your source code' is 10 words and exact on the home page (finding answered). I26: the note now has only the OpenSSL story claim; span 'Maintainers can trigger an AISLE review simply by tagging the aisle-analyzer handle' is exact on the OpenSSL customer page, grade documented, mode deployed, note says the account was not checked (answered). I18 and A4: no change, accepted; the available flag is kept and the response is true, span exact on the remediation page (answered). S1: note now says the named customer limb is what is counted and that no pull request or task count is published; Productboard, 56 repositories and the span 'Jira ticket creation, Slack notifications, and AI-powered pull requests' are exact on the customer page; scope fits by the named-customer limb (answered). I41: documented, counts toward no level, note says documented only (answered). The eleven passed statements (I04, I08, I10, I11, I21, I22, I38, I57, I58, I67, I68) were unchanged since round one; the show check finds every span in its source and under fifteen words. Part D: every page, figure and name in the notes (Productboard, 56 repositories, Claude Code, Cursor, OpenSSL, aisle-analyzer) is in a source of the scan, except curl and Samba as listed above. Round-one findings: 8 in total, 6 fully answered (I20, I26, I18/A4, S1, I41, the grouped pass), levels answered as a note; S4 answered in substance but with a false statement in the note.

Card A4 R2 C1 O2. Autonomy level four rests on I08 (the page says AISLE writes a patch, runs the customer's tests and opens a pull request), I10 (one integration sentence naming scanners, repositories and CI) and I18 (the remediation page says nothing reaches the main branch until a person on the customer's team merges, and that the customer sets how far AISLE goes per severity and repository). Removing I18 leaves Autonomy with no level, because I15, I16 and I07 are not credited; removing I10 gives A3; removing S4 changes nothing, since Reach three also needs I25. Everything is documented from vendor pages and mode available for I18, so the display should say A4 is read from vendor statements and is opt-in, with no default stated; nothing on the card is observed or measured.

Round-two findings: S4 answered (fetched fresh: the announcement post answers 200, published 2026-11-09 in its metadata; span 'Simply connect AISLE to an AI agent that supports the MCP standard' is 12 words and exact; read-only, five tools, OAuth or personal access token, Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and Cursor are all on the page; the 404 sentence is gone; the post is in the captures). not_credited answered (duplicate removed; entry says OpenSSL only; the OpenSSL vulnerabilities page has 40 mentions of Aisle Research and no mention of curl or Samba; the open-source page does show the aisle-security handle inside a graphic as the second entry says). Levels note answered in part by the studio as it said: I18 span 'Nothing reaches your main branch until someone on your team merges it.' is 12 words and exact on the remediation page, and the same page says 'You decide how far AISLE goes on its own, per severity and per repository', so the new note is true; grade documented, mode available, indicator I18 fit. The unchanged answers were re-found in their sources by the show check, spans under fifteen words. The gate prints OK (v0.0.92). Fully answered: 3 of 3 round-two findings (S4, not_credited, levels as a note), plus the grouped pass.

Process only, not a defect in the answer: the studio response says S4 must be re-captured with tools/capture.mjs before publication; the captures list now holds the announcement post, but the two not_credited sources (openssl-library.org vulnerabilities page and aisle.com/open-source) are not captured, which is acceptable as they credit nothing.

I04.n: The remediation FAQ states AISLE builds the repository in an isolated container, applies its patch and runs the tests.
I04.span: AISLE builds your repository in an isolated container, applies the patch

I08.n: The page states AISLE writes a patch, runs it against the customer's tests and opens a pull request.
I08.span: AISLE writes the patch, runs it against your own test suite

I10.n: The platform page states it plugs into the customer's scanners, repositories and CI.
I10.span: AISLE plugs into the scanners, repos, and CI you already run

I11.n: AISLE connects from its own service to the customer's hosted version control systems.
I11.span: AISLE connects to GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps.

I18.n: The page states AISLE writes and tests a patch and opens a pull request, that the customer decides per severity and repository how far it goes, and that a person on the customer's team merges; no default is stated.
I18.span: Nothing reaches your main branch until someone on your team merges it.

I20.n: The home page states what the system is for: finding, fixing and verifying vulnerabilities in source code.
I20.span: finds, fixes, and verifies vulnerabilities in your source code

I21.n: The customer sets how far AISLE acts on its own, per severity and per repository.
I21.span: You decide how far AISLE goes on its own

I22.n: The page states which findings get guidance instead of a patch, and that a fix breaking tests goes back to the team.
I22.span: When findings can't be safely patched, it provides clear remediation advice instead.

I26.n: AISLE's OpenSSL story states maintainers invoke it by tagging the GitHub handle @aisle-analyzer. Stated by AISLE; the account was not checked on GitHub.
I26.span: Maintainers can trigger an AISLE review simply by tagging @aisle-analyzer

I38.n: A merge to the main branch needs a person on the customer's team; AISLE opens the pull request and waits.
I38.span: it opens the pull request and waits for human approval

I41.n: The enterprise FAQ states every finding and fix is logged through to the approved pull request, with timestamps and approvers; documented only, not observed.
I41.span: every finding and fix is logged from detection to verified fix

I57.n: Users can contest a triage decision by explaining why and sending the issue back for re-assessment.
I57.span: just explain why and send the issue back through triage

I58.n: The privacy policy lists customer data as code repositories and related data submitted to the service.
I58.span: Code repositories and related data submitted to Services

I67.n: The enterprise page states a figure for engineering hours saved, and the remediation page gives monthly patch and hours figures; no method is published.
I67.span: AISLE has already saved teams 50,000+ engineering hours.

I68.n: The deployment comparison states updates and intel are continuous for Managed SaaS and delivered monthly for private cloud and on-prem; this is an update cadence, with no improvement process described.

S1.n: A customer story names Productboard, which rolled AISLE out across all 56 repositories and integrated its AI-powered pull requests into its workflow; the named customer is what is counted, as the page publishes no count of pull requests or tasks. CVE credits to Aisle Research name staff researchers and are not counted here.
S1.span: Jira ticket creation, Slack notifications, and AI-powered pull requests

S4.n: AISLE's announcement post, published 9 November 2026, states its MCP server gives a customer's coding agent, such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex or Cursor, read-only access to AISLE findings through five tools, with sign-in by OAuth or a personal access token.
S4.span: Simply connect AISLE to an AI agent that supports the MCP standard

not_credited.what: OpenSSL advisories credit vulnerabilities to researchers of Aisle Research.
not_credited.why: The credits name people, so they show AISLE's team at work, not the agent acting on its own.

not_credited.what: The open-source page shows an 'aisle-security' bot account inside a styled mock-up of a GitHub thread.
not_credited.why: A mock-up graphic, not a statement that the account exists; I26 rests on the OpenSSL story alone.

announced.what: Cohere to acquire AISLE (letter of intent signed 15 October 2026; completion not stated).
MCP server: more actions beyond read access are 'on the way'.

Headline figures: 650+ CVEs, 91% true positive rate, 85% fix acceptance, 4-day MTTR, '10x more cost-efficient than Mythos', 15,000+ engineering hours saved per month. Vendor figures, method not published on the page.
'#1' on the UC Berkeley Vulnerability Initiative leaderboard (the leaderboard data does list 'AISLE Research Team' with 514 in Volume).
